1. Ingress and Egress Rules
A security group's ingress rules control real, incoming traffic, egress rules control real, outgoing traffic, together defining exactly what network access is actually allowed.
Each rule specifies a real, actual port range, protocol, and source or destination, genuinely precise control over network access.
This is the real, primary mechanism controlling which resources can actually talk to which others, and from where, across an entire, live deployment.
Understanding this well is genuinely essential before deploying any real, live resource that needs to communicate over a network at all.
This topic assumes the VPC and subnets already covered in the previous two topics, every security group here attaches to resources living inside them.
By the end of this topic, real, live network access should feel like a genuinely deliberate, well-reasoned decision, not a broad, convenient default.

This genuinely scales cleanly, adding a new, real allowed port becomes a one-line change to the underlying list, not a whole, new, repeated block.

blocks.content: 3. Least Privilege, Applied Directly
Recall Least Privilege from the Security module, applied directly here, a real security group should allow exactly the real, necessary traffic, and genuinely nothing more.
This is the exact same principle already covered abstractly, now tied to actual, live, real network rules protecting genuine, running infrastructure.
Opening only the real, specific ports a resource actually needs, rather than a broad, convenient range, is this principle in genuinely direct action.
This connects the Security module's closing, unifying principle directly to one of the most common, real, everyday resources it actually applies to.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555858451-735012293.png

blocks.content: 4. A Real, Complete Example
A real, complete security group example opens only the real, necessary ports, 443 for HTTPS, for instance, and genuinely nothing else, by deliberate, real design.
This is worth treating as a genuine, real starting template, adapted directly to whatever specific, real ports a given resource actually needs.
Every practice in this topic individually comes together here, real, precise rules, applying least privilege, deliberately and directly.
This exact pattern, minimal and deliberate, is worth applying consistently to every real security group covered throughout this module.
5. One Security Group Referencing Another
A real, genuinely cleaner practice has one security group's rule reference another security group directly, rather than a broad, real CIDR range.
This means only real, specific resources, exactly those in the referenced security group, can actually reach this one, genuinely tighter access than any CIDR range.
This real, common pattern, a database security group allowing traffic only from a real, specific application security group, is genuinely worth adopting broadly.
This is a real, concrete, practical expression of least privilege, applied specifically at the level of security group design.
This pattern also genuinely simplifies real, later changes, adding a new instance to the referenced security group automatically grants it the same, real access.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555862703-19461615.png
blocks.alt: A real, common, genuinely cleaner practice, tighter than any real CIDR range could achieve

blocks.content:
resource "aws_security_group_rule" "db_from_app" {
  type                     = "ingress"
  from_port                = 5432
  to_port                  = 5432
  protocol                 = "tcp"
  security_group_id        = aws_security_group.db.id
  source_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id
}

blocks.content: 6. Security Groups Are Genuinely Stateful
Security groups are genuinely stateful, real return traffic for an already-allowed connection is automatically permitted, no separate, matching egress rule genuinely needed.
This is worth understanding clearly, it explains why a real, working configuration often needs fewer explicit rules than might initially seem necessary.
This real, stateful behavior differs from network ACLs, a related but genuinely separate AWS concept, beyond this topic's specific, real scope.
Understanding this distinction avoids a real, common confusion when reasoning about exactly why certain, real traffic is or is not actually allowed.
This genuinely simplifies most, real, everyday security group design, focus on ingress rules, egress is often left permissive by default, or genuinely narrowed deliberately.
This small, real, structural detail is worth remembering, it explains a genuinely common early surprise about how few explicit rules a working setup needs.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555864293-752184466.png
blocks.alt: Genuinely stateful, real return traffic automatically allowed, no extra rule genuinely needed

blocks.content: 7. A Real, Genuinely Dangerous Mistake
0.0.0.0/0, opening a real port to the entire internet, is a real, genuinely dangerous, common mistake, worth using only when truly, deliberately necessary.
This is genuinely appropriate for a real, public-facing web server's HTTPS port, and genuinely inappropriate for nearly everything else in a live deployment.
The honest fix is scoping ingress rules to genuinely specific, real sources, another security group, or a real, known IP range, wherever possible.
This mistake is worth flagging immediately in any real code review, exactly the scrutiny already covered for IAM policy changes.

blocks.alt: A real, genuinely dangerous, common mistake, worth using only when truly, deliberately necessary

8. A Real, Practical Checklist
Before applying any real, new security group rule, a short, honest checklist genuinely helps confirm it follows the practices covered throughout this topic.
Confirming the real, specific port, the narrowest genuinely possible source, and a real, clear reason for the rule existing covers the large majority of real risk.
This checklist is worth running through for every new, real security group rule, not just the first one a project ever creates.
Building it into a real, shared team practice keeps security group hygiene consistent across an entire, real, live deployment.

blocks.content: 9. A Real, Multi-Tier Example
A genuinely real, multi-tier application uses separate security groups per tier, web, application, and database, each referencing the one above it directly.
The web tier accepts real, public HTTPS traffic, the app tier accepts traffic only from the web tier's security group, the database tier only from the app tier.
This layered, real pattern directly applies the security-group-referencing-security-group practice already covered, at the scale of a genuine, complete application.
This is worth treating as a real, practical template for structuring security groups in any genuinely real, multi-tier deployment.

["Web tier: accepts real, public HTTPS traffic directly.","App tier: accepts traffic only from the web tier's security group.","Database tier: accepts traffic only from the app tier's security group."]

App tier: accepts traffic only from the web tier's security group.
Database tier: accepts traffic only from the app tier's security group.

Recall the periodic review discipline already covered in Least Privilege, security group rules deserve the exact same, real, recurring, honest scrutiny.
A rule added once for a genuinely real, but now-obsolete need can quietly remain in place indefinitely, unless actively, deliberately reviewed.
A real, periodic audit, checking every rule against a genuinely current, real need, keeps a live security posture honestly aligned with actual, current usage.

points: Security groups control real network access through ingress and egress rules, genuinely stateful, return traffic is automatically allowed.
Apply least privilege directly, real ports and sources scoped to exactly what is genuinely needed, referencing other security groups where possible.
